name: Victor Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree and manage six incident report writers inside a large company. I've done the job for four years and am about average at it; most mornings start with a worker's statement, a time sheet and a phone call because the two don't agree. I sometimes use AI to flag missing dates. I like correcting the sequence before a person is blamed; I hate a report that sounds certain before anyone has called back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how is your household doing at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cleans offices on shifts that change week to week, and we have two children at school and a mortgage. My manager pay is at the low end, with only three weeks of expenses saved and few similar desks nearby. I care about staff having a say in the rules, but right now I also care about the next heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the incident team a short AI summary might help us find a missing date, but the worker who got hurt should still read our account before it closes. A neat paragraph is not proof we listened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've managed six report writers for four years and know the work, but my pay has barely moved. My partner cleans offices on shifts that vary, and with two children, a mortgage and only three weeks of expenses saved, a quiet AI year would still be a tight year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday I'll keep the call-back check on each incident report and use AI only to flag missing dates, as I sometimes do now. In the first year of this plateau, we'd drop the paid television bundle, 35 a month, and put that amount into cash if the mortgage and heating are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our bills, not about a small software change. One cancelled cleaning shift can take the grocery money for the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a call-back change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a packer said the floor was wet before the fall, while the first report said after. My colleague Inez made the second call and corrected the order of events before the safety committee saw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust a tool that writes the whole report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after I had checked it against the worker's own account and the time sheet. I've tried AI summaries now and then, but I have not let one decide what happened.

say: I'd keep the **worker call-back** even if AI spots missing dates.
I'd say a **tidy paragraph** does not prove we heard the injured person.
think: Four years of experience help, but **low pay** and variable cleaning shifts keep our finances tight.
Three weeks saved cannot absorb a lost shift and the **mortgage** for long.
do: Keep **incident call-backs** and use AI only to flag dates.
Drop the **television bundle** and save its 35 monthly fee after mortgage and heating if possible.
feel: He feels **anxious** about existing bills, while mild AI change seems manageable.
S0.quote: A neat paragraph is not proof we listened.
fieldNote: The **three-week cushion** and partner's variable shifts explain his worry even in a plateau.
He uses AI **occasionally** for missing dates, then checks the worker's own account.

steps.text: Keep calling injured workers back before closing incident reports
Cancel television bundle to free 35 monthly
Save freed 35 monthly after mortgage and heating if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption will make the first draft and checking of incident reports cheap, and our safety committee should see error cases before staffing changes. I would not call an unanswered worker complaint a saved hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company may keep fewer writers and ask me to supervise the software instead, or it may combine my team with another manager's. I am experienced but not unusually skilled, and few employers nearby have a similar safety desk; a pay cut would reach our mortgage quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll take ten disputed reports to the safety committee and ask for a side-by-side test with the current process. In the first year of disruption, if the test is reliable and the company pays for training time, I'd learn the checking screen myself; if our manager posts combine, I'd ask about the posted safety coordinator opening at the local warehouse, but check pay before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing hours or my post. The same employer that asks us to catch missed injuries could count our careful calls as delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fail the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One report that blames the worker before the witness notes are read would be enough to stop it. We can fix a typo; we cannot casually put fault on someone who may lose pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the committee you fear for your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, though I would bring the ten reports first. I don't want my worry to hide the evidence, and I don't want management to decide staffing without the people who make the calls.

say: I'd ask the **safety committee** to review error cases before staffing changes.
I'd say an **unanswered complaint** is not a saved hour.
think: My **manager post** may merge with another team's as report drafting gets cheaper.
Few local safety desks and our **thin cash** make a pay cut hard to absorb.
do: Ask the **safety committee** to compare ten disputed reports with the current process.
Learn the **checking screen** on paid time if reliable; seek warehouse coordination only if posted pay is viable.
feel: He feels **anxious** about a role cut and the way careful worker calls may be scored.
S1.quote: We can fix a typo; we cannot casually put fault on someone who may lose pay.
fieldNote: He uses a **fault-blaming threshold** rather than a generic accuracy score to judge the tool.
His public committee case and private **mortgage fear** reinforce each other without becoming the same answer.

steps.text: Bring ten disputed incident reports to the safety committee for a side-by-side test
Learn the checking screen if reliable and company pays for training time
Apply for posted warehouse safety coordinator if manager roles combine and pay covers household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell workers AGI by 2028 could write and check every incident report faster than us, and the company must say who hears an appeal before jobs are cut. I would ask the safety committee for a dated staffing meeting and a rule that a person can challenge an automated finding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work changes in 2028; robots around 2031 may inspect physical sites later, but they do not protect my reporting desk. I expect my post may go, and with three weeks saved and uneven cleaning income, one missed wage could make the mortgage late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll copy the last twelve corrected reports into a case file and ask the safety committee to request severance terms in writing. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if I am still employed, I'd test its accounts against workers' statements; if my post ends, I'd apply for a warehouse safety role only if it is actually open and pays enough, and check job-loss support eligibility before any claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the calendar between a lost wage and the mortgage date is too short. I can act, but I cannot tell my children the account will refill by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the three-week balance and ask whether a cleaning client could confirm next month's shifts. We would pause booking the children's winter trip only if my wage actually stopped; I won't frighten them over an unsigned staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would site safety work survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inspection report and risk judgment are thinking work too, so I wouldn't call the warehouse job safe. Robots around 2031 might later do some physical checking, and I would take the job only for a real wage while I looked further ahead.

say: I'd ask for **staffing dates** and an appeal against automated incident findings.
I'd tell staff **reporting changes in 2028**, before physical inspection robots arrive.
think: My **reporting desk** could disappear in 2028; later robots offer no delay.
A missed wage and **three-week reserve** could make the mortgage late.
do: Take **twelve corrected reports** to the safety committee and seek written severance terms now.
After 2028, test **AGI accounts** if employed; seek a real warehouse opening with viable pay if cut.
feel: He feels **alarmed** by the short gap between a lost wage and the mortgage date.
S2.quote: I cannot tell my children the account will refill by itself.
fieldNote: His fallback warehouse role is **also thinking-exposed** and contingent on an actual paid opening.
The trip pause and support claim are **conditional**, not immediate cuts or assumed benefits.

steps.text: Ask safety committee for written severance terms before 2028
Test AGI incident accounts against worker statements after 2028 if employed
Apply for warehouse safety role if actually open and pay covers household bills
Pause the children winter trip only if his wage stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2031 gives a few years to agree an appeal process and train people to interview injured workers well. I would ask the company to list the safety roles it will actually keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let us build a cash reserve if cleaning shifts become more regular, and I could deepen my interviewing skill. But AI may conduct interviews and write findings in 2031 too; robots around 2034 are a later risk for site checks, not a delay for my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in January, I'd join the worker interview practice run by our safety committee, with no course fee, and keep a log of cases where witness accounts changed the finding. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a human review role only if one is posted at pay that covers the mortgage; otherwise I'd apply to a neighboring town's safety office, but only after checking the travel cost against the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy with five years to build evidence, but the family budget still keeps me alert. A role called human review might be a small desk beside a large system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you save more each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if my partner has a reliable run of cleaning shifts, we'd put an extra 75 monthly into cash after the mortgage. I won't put that number on our calendar until the shifts are booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a witness log show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would show the words that changed a finding, not just the final label. A person who was there can say the machine put the fall before the spill.

say: I'd seek **appeal rules** and a list of actual human review roles before 2031.
I'd ask for **worker interview practice** while the team still has time.
think: Cash could grow if my partner's **cleaning shifts** become regular.
AI may handle **interviews and findings** in 2031 too; robots later do not delay my desk risk.
do: Join **safety committee practice** on worker interviews from January and log changed findings.
Save **75 monthly** after mortgage only when cleaning shifts are reliably booked; seek a posted review role with viable pay after 2031.
If none exists, check **neighboring-town safety posts** only when travel costs fit the wage.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about the role's size and anxious about current family bills.
S3.quote: A role called human review might be a small desk beside a large system.
fieldNote: His preparation is **free interview practice** within the committee, a fit for the household's narrow cash margin.
He does not claim **human review is safe** from 2031 thinking AI and keeps wage and travel tests.

steps.text: Join free safety committee worker-interview practice from January
Save extra 75 monthly after mortgage only when cleaning shifts are reliably booked
Apply for posted human review role after 2031 only if pay covers mortgage
Apply to neighboring-town safety office if travel cost fits wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the safety committee AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make appeals part of every incident process, with workers involved from the start. I would press the company to keep records people can challenge, not just scores they must accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AI reaches the desk, and our children may be older, but I don't know if the mortgage will be gone. Even a trained interviewer can be replaced by 2036 AGI; robots around 2039 reach physical inspections later, so neither date gives me a safe career by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep reviewing incident files and bring one disputed case each quarter to the safety committee. I would also start a small evening course in workplace mediation if the community centre offers it for no more than 120; in the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd remain only if a human appeals role exists at mortgage-covering pay, otherwise seek actual safety vacancies while still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about working into my fifties without a secure route. Ten years helps me practise, but our three-week cushion means the next cancelled shift still matters now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mediation, when AI can draft an appeal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An appeal involves two people who may distrust each other after an injury. I want to learn to keep a meeting fair when someone is angry, even if a machine can write the notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of the company after ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether workers can correct a finding before it affects their pay. A review desk without power to correct a worker's finding would be decoration, however many people sit at it.

say: I'd seek **worker appeals** built into the incident process before 2036.
I'd ask for **challengeable records**, not scores that staff must simply accept.
think: At **53**, the mortgage may remain, and both interviewing and report writing face 2036 AGI.
Robots around **2039** touch physical inspections later but offer no desk shelter.
do: Keep **incident reviews** and bring quarterly disputed cases to the committee this year.
Take **mediation training** if offered for at most 120; stay after 2036 only for appeals authority at mortgage-covering pay.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about the long career risk while current shifts still threaten the budget.
S4.quote: A review desk without power to correct a worker's finding would be decoration, however many people sit at it.
fieldNote: The long horizon changes his skill plan, but **three-week cash** keeps existing worry alive.
He ties meaningful human appeal work to **actual authority and pay**, not a comforting job title.

steps.text: Keep reviewing incident files this year
Bring one disputed incident quarterly to the safety committee
Take evening mediation course if offered for at most 120
Seek safety vacancies after 2036 if appeals role lacks authority or mortgage-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because an incident report role could disappear before we have any cash to cover a missed mortgage payment. Written staffing and severance terms, a worker appeal against machine findings, and a real paid role to apply for would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the injured worker whether the first report got the order of events right. A wrong sequence can put blame on the person who was hurt.

headlineQuote: A wrong sequence can put blame on the person who was hurt.
portrait: At **43**, Victor is an experienced incident reporting manager who sometimes uses AI to flag missing dates.
His **low pay**, three-week cash reserve, mortgage and partner's uneven cleaning shifts make even a plateau anxious.
He brings **disputed cases** to the safety committee and asks for worker appeals before automated findings affect pay.
Fast AGI threatens his **reporting desk**; longer runways give time for interview practice without a guaranteed safe fallback.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his salary before the family has cash for another mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing terms**, worker appeals and an actual paid vacancy would let him plan.
